name: Dɔ̃
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Blench, Roger. 2006. The Dɔ̃ (Dong) language and its affinities. Draft manuscript, printout 20 November 2006. Cambridge: Mallam Dendo. 17 pp. (Glottolog ref 134940; PDF from the author's site via the Internet Archive)
catalog_locator: Sec. 2 Phonology, subsection 'Tones', p. 2; caveat sentence p. 1
catalog_quote: Tones The tone system of Dɔ̃ is quite restricted with many words having all level tones. I have transcribed two tones. No cases of glide tones seem to occur on the tapes. In cases where I am uncertain, the tone is left unmarked.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (17 pp., A4, Distiller metadata 'Microsoft Word - Dong wordlist.DOC', author Roger M Blench, created 2006-11-20; footer 'This printout: November 20, 2006'). extracted text of p. 3 (printed p. 2) gives the 'Tones' paragraph exactly as quoted: 'The tone system of Dɔ̃ is quite restricted with many words having all level tones. I have transcribed two tones. No cases of glide tones seem to occur on the tapes. In cases where I am uncertain, the tone is left unmarked.' Verbatim match. Sec. 2 'Phonology' (printed pp. 1-2) consists only of: a caveat that the phonology 'is based on rapid observations and a taped wordlist' and is 'tentative', an 8-vowel chart, a consonant chart with a note on f…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dong is described as a (restricted) two-tone language on the basis of a taped wordlist; the only description in existence says nothing at all about word stress or accent. No stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author flags the whole phonology as 'tentative', based on 'rapid observations and a taped wordlist' (p. 1).
new_statements.domain_note: Citation-form wordlist items only (c. 300 lexical items with tone marks); no phrase-level or grammatical description exists.
new_statements.identity_note: The one source describes the Dɔ̃ speech of Dong village, Taraba State, Nigeria (elicited from one speaker, Peter Dong, Jos 1993, plus items from an NBTT Mumuye dialect survey); this is dong1293 [doh] itself, no dialect issue. Note that Glottolog's reference list for doh includes Long & Zheng 1998 'The Dong Language in Guizhou Province, China', which is a misattribution (Kam, Kam-Tai, China) and was not examined.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2006. The Dɔ̃ (Dong) language and its affinities. Draft manuscript, printout 20 November 2006. Cambridge: Mallam Dendo. 17 pp.
sources.quote: The tone system of Dɔ̃ is quite restricted with many words having all level tones. I have transcribed two tones. No cases of glide tones seem to occur on the tapes. In cases where I am uncertain, the tone is left unmarked.
sources.note: Sec. 2 'Phonology' (printed pp. 1-2; pp. 2-3) gives 8 vowels, a consonant chart and a 'Tones' paragraph (p. 2): two level tones transcribed, no glide tones on the tapes, tone left unmarked where uncertain; phonology explicitly 'tentative', from a taped wordlist. The words stress/accent do not occur anywhere in the 17 pages (a full-text search for stress/accent full text).
